oneliner.t: Emergency physician and former Arizona state representative (2019–Feb 2024) from Phoenix; the 2024 Democratic nominee, he lost AZ-01 to David Schweikert 51.9%–48.1%, then won the July 21, 2026 Democratic primary over DCCC-backed Marlene Galán-Woods by about 3,700 votes. He faces Republican Jay Feely and Libertarian Monica Alponte.

born.t: 1977 or 1978 (exact date not documented), Chicago, Illinois
born.note: Both sources give Chicago. Wikipedia's infobox gives only an age range (48–49).

upbringing.t: Raised in Chicago. His Gujarati parents immigrated from India in the 1960s while pursuing engineering degrees; his father is Jain and his mother Hindu. He earned a B.A. in economics (1997) and an M.D. (2001) at Northwestern, then an M.P.H. at UC Berkeley (2003). After an emergency-medicine residency in New York City and faculty work at Mount Sinai, he moved to Arizona for a sports-medicine fellowship at the University of Arizona and later practiced at Mayo Clinic Arizona. He entered politics after a Scottsdale meeting encouraged him to run, and campaigned door to door at the urging of then-House minority leader Eric Meyer.

career.role: Emergency-medicine resident (New York City), then faculty and researcher

career.yrs: 2008–2009 seasons (AP, per his campaign); Wikipedia says five seasons

career.role: Emergency physician (salary $227,913.93 in 2025; $84,825 in 2026 to mid-July)
State representative, LD24 (2019–2023) and LD5 (2023–Feb 2024); ranking member, Health & Human Services in his final term
Contract emergency physician (The Emergency Center; US Acute Care Solutions); president, AMS Emergency Services LLC; board member, Arizona College of Emergency Physicians

platform.t: Health care: his 2024 site backed universal health care; he campaigns on lowering health-care and prescription-drug costs. KJZZ reports he has never said he supports a government-run (socialized) system.

Abortion: his 2024 site called him '100% pro-choice' and said he personally gathered more than 1,200 signatures for the abortion-access ballot initiative. His 2026 home page lists abortion rights among the things he would defend.
Housing/education: supports wider pre-K access and federal incentives for affordable housing in Arizona; his 2024 site called for higher teacher pay and school funding.
Border: supports securing the U.S.–Mexico border.
Democracy: his 2024 site pledged to oppose gerrymandering and the influence of money in politics.
Israel: backs a two-state solution and Iron Dome/defensive weapons for Israel; criticized Israel's current prime minister (June 2026 forum). Details in the israel block.

promises.t: Accept no contributions from corporate PACs.
Defend Social Security, Medicare, abortion rights and the rule of law.

claims.claim: Won three straight elections to the Arizona State House (2018, 2020, 2022).

record.t: Elected in two-seat legislative districts in 2018 (LD24), 2020 (LD24, 35.9%) and 2022 (LD5, 40.3%).

claims.claim: Served five years in the State Legislature.

record.t: Took office Jan 14, 2019 and resigned Feb 1, 2024 to run for Congress: just over five years.

claims.claim: Had more bills signed into law than any Arizona Democrat in the last decade.
claims.short: Most bills signed by a Democrat

said.where: campaign About page and home page

record.t: Wikipedia lists his enacted bills from 2019–2023 (vehicle registration fees, prior-authorization forms, EMT transport, HIV-test consent, cat declawing, and others) but gives no comparison. J Street PAC repeats the claim. No independent tally of Arizona Democrats' enacted bills was found.

claims.claim: Has worked as an emergency-room physician for more than two decades.

record.t: M.D. 2001 (Ballotpedia), followed by an emergency-medicine residency. The year he began practicing is not documented. His 2026 disclosure confirms he still earns income practicing medicine.

claims.claim: Board-certified in emergency medicine and still practices in the district.

record.t: Current practice is confirmed: 2026 income from Mayo Clinic, The Emergency Center and US Acute Care Solutions. Board certification and practice location were not checked against a certification registry.

claims.claim: Provided sideline emergency care for the New York Jets as an NFL physician.

record.t: AP: airway-management physician at Jets home games in the 2008 and 2009 seasons, per his campaign. Wikipedia: team physician for five seasons while at Mount Sinai. The two sources differ on length of service.

claims.claim: As a state representative he represented key parts of the 1st Congressional District.

record.t: He represented LD24 and LD5 in Phoenix. District overlap with CD1 was not checked against redistricting maps.

claims.claim: Has personally knocked on more than 28,000 doors in AZ-01.

record.t: No independent record. His 2024 site claimed 'nearly 20,000' doors.

claims.claim: His campaign accepts no contributions from corporate PACs.

record.t: FEC: $146,250 from other (non-party) committees in 2025–26 and $480,244.58 in 2023–24. FEC summaries do not separate corporate PACs from other PACs, and the itemized list was not opened.

claims.claim: Said he was 'proud to earn the endorsement of the Independent Party of Arizona.'

record.t: No legal party by that name exists in Arizona. His spokesperson said he meant the No Labels Party, whose attempt to rename itself the 'Arizona Independent Party' a court blocked after the two major parties sued. No Labels' chair said he does not think Shah is misleading voters; the RNC called it a trick.

said.t: Says he works across party lines and is an independent voice.

did.t: KJZZ: as a legislator he broke ranks with the Democratic caucus at times; primary rivals and former Rep. Raquel Terán said he frustrated Democrats by working with Republicans.

aipac_endorse.t: Not checked directly (AIPAC's endorsement portal not opened). In 2024, AIPAC's PAC endorsed his opponent, Schweikert.

aipac_pac.note: Not documented. Track AIPAC's Congress page covers sitting members only; he is not listed.

udp.note: No direct UDP spending documented; a UDP spokesperson said UDP had 'no involvement in any way in AZ-1' (Jul 2026). UDP did give money to two super PACs that spent against him in the 2026 primary (see others).

others.name: DMFI PAC (Democratic Majority for Israel's political arm): backed his 2024 general-election campaign; amount not stated. JDCA's Arizona chapter also endorsed him.
JStreetPAC: endorsed him as a 'Priority' candidate for 2026 and listed an Oct 8, 2026 Phoenix reception; amount not stated
BOLD America: spent 'just under $1 million' AGAINST him in the 2026 primary; it received $650,000 from UDP in May 2026
Crush MAGA: spent 'over half a million dollars' AGAINST him (and for Jonathan Treble) in the 2026 primary; it is an affiliate of Save Democracy PAC, which received $100,000 from UDP
Republican Jewish Coalition Victory Fund: supported Schweikert against him in 2024; amount not stated

statements.t: Said a 2019 trip to Israel as a state legislator helped shape his worldview.

A Middle East position paper (drafted April 2024) supports continued U.S. aid to Israel with no additional restrictions and backs Israel's fight against Hamas. It voices sorrow over civilian deaths in Gaza, citing his Jain faith's pacifism, and faults the lack of international pressure to dismantle Hamas.

At a June 18 forum he said he strongly supports a two-state solution and fully backs Iron Dome and other defensive weapons for Israel. He also said the current Israeli prime minister's policies are weakening Israeli society and making Israel less secure.
JStreetPAC says he stands with J Street on a 'pro-peace, pro-Israel' agenda.

corp.t: Non-party committees (PACs) gave $146,250 in 2025–26 and $480,244.58 in 2023–24. The FEC summaries do not split business PACs from ideological ones, and the itemized list was not opened, so his 'no corporate PAC money' pledge is unverified. No corporate-funded super PAC was found spending for him.

lobby.t: Against him in the 2026 primary: BOLD America, which received $650K from UDP in May, spent just under $1M opposing him. Crush MAGA, a vehicle of Save Democracy PAC (which received $100K from UDP), spent over $500K combined opposing him and backing Jonathan Treble. Pro-Choice Majority Action, funded mainly by EDW Action Fund (which received $1M from UDP), backed Marlene Galan-Woods, whom DMFI PAC also backed. UDP said it had 'no involvement in any way in AZ-1', and the record does not show that UDP money was earmarked for this race.

trades.note: Candidate reports have no transaction schedule. Holdings are almost all mutual funds and index funds in retirement accounts. He never sat on a congressional committee.

note.t: Assets: 401(k)/403(b)/IRA mutual funds (largest Vanguard Explorer Fund $500K–$1M, Vanguard Institutional Index $250K–$500K, Fidelity 500 Index $250K–$500K), TIAA Traditional, an Arizona state retirement 401(a), an HSA, and a $1–$1,000 stake in ReferWell, a small medical-referral startup. Earned income: Mayo Clinic salary ($227,913.93 in 2025), The Emergency Center ($102,220 in 2025) and US Acute Care Solutions ($4,320). No liabilities.

note.t: Raised in Chicago. He came to Arizona for a University of Arizona fellowship (year not documented) and represented Phoenix legislative districts 2019–2024. He lives in Phoenix; whether his home is inside AZ-01 was not documented.

research_notes: The primary margin (~3,700 votes, about 39%–34%) is from KJZZ and the Algemeiner; az-races.json has 39.4%–34.4%. The DCCC endorsed Galán-Woods in May 2026 and switched to Shah after the primary (Red to Blue, Jul 28). Feely and the NRCC call Shah a socialist; he does not use that label, and KJZZ notes his primary rivals attacked him as too conservative. AP notes Shah worked Jets home games during Feely's 2008–09 Jets seasons. Ballotpedia's 2026 section is stale (it lists an Aug 4 primary).
